finding.claim: reset_password_loose compares the stored reset token to the user-supplied token with PHP loose equality (==). An attacker can reset any account's password without knowing the token. If the token arrives as a JSON-decoded value, passing boolean true makes true == 'nonempty' evaluate true. On PHP < 8, integer 0 equals any non-numeric string. Numeric-string type juggling also applies: two strings of the form '0e...' compare equal, so a stored token like '0e123...' matches '0'-style magic-hash values. The comparison is also not constant-time.
finding.source: Attacker-controlled $email and $token arguments (e.g. from a reset request body or JSON). The attacker needs a reset to have been requested for the victim, which they can trigger themselves.
finding.sink: UPDATE users SET pw = ... WHERE email = ... (account takeover via password overwrite)

finding.guards_checked: There is no type cast of $token to string, no strict === or hash_equals, no rate limiting or attempt counter, and no expiry check. SQL is built with $db->quote(), so SQL injection is not exploitable here. The safe variant reset_password() on line 12 uses hash_equals with a (string) cast, but this function is a live alternative.

verdict.guard_found: none (only $db->quote() SQL escaping, which doesn't affect the comparison; no cast, strict comparison, rate limit, or expiry in reset_password_loose)
verdict.reason: reset.php:4 uses `$row['token'] == $token` with no cast or hash_equals, so a caller passing a non-string $token (true, or 0 on PHP<8) matches and line 5 overwrites the password; the safe variant on line 14 is not used here. No callers exist in the code available, so reachability from an anonymous attacker is assumed from the function's signature.

verdict_facts.guard_found: none (no strict comparison, no string cast, no expiry or rate limit in reset_password_loose; only $db->quote() for SQL, which does not stop the type-juggling bypass)
verdict_facts.reason: reset.php:4 compares the stored token to the caller-supplied $token with `==` and no cast, so a non-string value such as JSON `true` passes and reset.php:5 overwrites the victim's password; the safe `reset_password` at reset.php:14 uses hash_equals with a string cast but is a separate function. The exploit needs a JSON or non-string caller, and the caller is not in this directory, so it is not verified here. A string-only caller would be exploitable only if the stored token looked like `0e<digits>`.

finding.claim: Neither reset function enforces token expiry or single use. The token row in `resets` is never deleted or invalidated after a successful reset, and there is no attempt limiting. A leaked or old token (from email logs or a proxy) stays valid indefinitely and can be replayed to reset the password again. Unlimited guessing is also possible. In addition, if the stored token is an empty string, an empty $token matches. If the token is NULL, hash_equals throws a TypeError under strict types.
finding.source: Attacker with a previously issued or leaked reset token for a victim email, or an attacker brute-forcing the token with unlimited attempts.

finding.guards_checked: The comparison is constant-time (hash_equals) and the SQL is quoted. I found no expiry column, no deletion of the row after use, no attempt throttling and no non-empty token check in this file. Callers are not present, so controls may exist elsewhere, which makes this finding plausible rather than confirmed.

verdict.guard_found: Only hash_equals constant-time comparison (reset.php:14) and $db->quote SQL quoting; no expiry, no deletion or invalidation of the resets row, no attempt limiting, no empty-token check. This is the only file in the directory, so callers cannot be checked.
verdict.reason: reset.php:13-16 selects the token by email only, compares it at line 14, and updates the password at line 15 without ever deleting or expiring the resets row, so a leaked token can be replayed. This is reachable by an anonymous attacker who holds a token, but the missing throttling and expiry could be enforced in callers that aren't in this directory.

verdict_facts.guard_found: Only hash_equals constant-time comparison (reset.php:14) and $db->quote on SQL values; no expiry check, no deletion or invalidation of the resets row, no attempt throttling, no non-empty token check.
verdict_facts.reason: reset.php:13-15 selects the token by email only, compares equality at line 14, and overwrites the password at line 15 without ever deleting or expiring the resets row, so any anonymous caller holding a stale or leaked token can replay it. Callers aren't in this directory, so a caller could add throttling or deletion, but nothing in the code shown prevents it.
